sections.markdown:
## C — Distracted driving, emotions and electronic devices

FACT_ID: sec12-F01 | anchor: A01
Studies show that anything that takes attention away from driving can result in a crash, and distracted drivers all show the same basic behavior of reacting more slowly to events such as a vehicle stopping to turn left or pulling out from a side road [A01].
Why it matters: Slower reaction is the common thread.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0055]

FACT_ID: sec12-F02 | anchor: A02
Distracted drivers more often fail to notice hazards such as pedestrians, bicyclists or debris, and they shrink their margin of safety, taking risks like turning left in front of oncoming traffic [A02].
Why it matters: Missed hazards and a thinner safety margin.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F03 | anchor: A02
Inattention and failure to yield are the most common driver actions contributing to pedestrian and bicycle crashes in Vermont [A02].
Why it matters: The two leading driver causes in Vermont.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F04 | anchor: A02
Pre program your favorite radio stations and keep the stereo low enough to hear sounds outside the vehicle such as a siren, a horn or a train whistle [A02].
Why it matters: Hearing outside sounds is a safety function.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F05 | anchor: A02
Let a front seat passenger act as co pilot instead of fumbling with maps or navigation, and when driving alone map the destination in advance [A02].
Why it matters: Navigation is delegated or done before leaving.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F06 | anchor: A02
Avoid eating and drinking while driving, keep food items secure and make sure drinks fit firmly in cup holders [A02].
Why it matters: Food is a named distraction.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F07 | anchor: A02
Do not underestimate how distracting children can be in the vehicle, and teach them the importance of good behavior while riding [A02].
Why it matters: Children are a managed distraction.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F08 | anchor: A02
Take a break if you find yourself lost in thought while driving, and focus on driving rather than people or objects inside or outside the vehicle [A02].
Why it matters: Daydreaming counts as distraction.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F09 | anchor: A02
Do personal grooming at home rather than in the vehicle, keep pets in a carrier rather than in your lap or loose, and avoid smoking while driving because it is a distraction [A02].
Why it matters: Grooming, pets and smoking are all named.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F10 | anchor: A02
Emotions affect safe driving, and you may not drive well when overly worried, excited, afraid, angry or depressed, so give yourself time to cool off and calm down, for example by taking a walk [A02].
Why it matters: Five named emotional states.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F11 | anchor: A02
Plan ahead and leave a few minutes early, because a driver with plenty of time is less likely to speed, break laws or crash [A02].
Why it matters: Extra time reduces rule breaking.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F12 | anchor: A02
It is against the law for a driver to read or send messages while driving [A02].
Why it matters: The texting ban in one sentence.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F13 | anchor: A02
Vermont law forbids a driver from using a portable electronic device while operating a vehicle on a public highway, and the ban still applies when the vehicle is stopped [A02].
Why it matters: Stopped in traffic still counts.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F14 | anchor: A02
A first violation of the portable electronic device law carries a fine of at least one hundred dollars and at most two hundred dollars, and a second or later violation a fine of at least two hundred fifty dollars and at most five hundred dollars [A02].
Why it matters: Two fine ranges.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F15 | anchor: A02
A conviction for using a portable electronic device while driving in a properly designated work zone with construction, maintenance or utility personnel present adds two points to the driving record for a first conviction and five points for a second or later conviction [A02].
Why it matters: Work zone device use adds points.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

FACT_ID: sec12-F16 | anchor: A02
Driving requires full attention, so if a call must be made ask a passenger to place it or stop at a safe place first [A02].
Why it matters: Passenger or pull over.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0056]

Misconceptions:
- Texting at a red light is legal because the car is not moving: false, the device ban covers a stationary vehicle on a public highway.
- A hands free rule means phones are fine as long as you do not text: false, the law bars use of a portable electronic device while operating the vehicle, and the handbook says to let a passenger call or pull over.
- Device points apply to every violation: false, points attach only to convictions in a designated work zone with workers present.
- Only phones distract: false, the handbook names food, children, pets, grooming, smoking, loud stereos and strong emotions as distractions.

Mnemonics:
- Hundred to two hundred first, two fifty to five hundred next: the device fine ranges.
- Two then five in the zone: work zone points for a first and a repeat device conviction.
- Passenger or pull over: the only two ways to make a call.

Glossary:
- Portable electronic device: a handheld device such as a phone, tablet or laptop whose use is barred while operating a vehicle on a public highway, even when stopped
- Margin of safety: the cushion of time and space a driver keeps against surprises, which distraction shrinks
- Designated work zone: a properly marked highway area with construction, maintenance or utility workers present, where device convictions add points

Dynamic facts isolated:
- None: every rule in this section is stable handbook law for the pined edition; no officeholder, date or fee amount is carried as knowledge.
